"'''Hold On'''" is a song by American [[girl group]] [[En Vogue]], released in February 1990 by [[Atlantic Records]] as the first single from their debut album, ''[[Born to Sing (En Vogue album)|Born to Sing]]'' (1990). It was produced by [[Denzil Foster]] and [[Thomas McElroy]], and written by the former two and all members of the group. It peaked at number two on the US [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] and topped the ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' [[Dance Club Songs|Dance Club Play]], [[Dance Singles Sales|12-inch Singles Sales]], and [[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs|Hot Black Singles]] charts. Internationally, "Hold On" entered the top 10 in the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. Its accompanying music video was directed by [[Tarsem Singh]]. En Vogue performed "Hold On" at the [[2008 BET Awards]] with [[Alicia Keys]]. In 2017, it was ranked number four on ''[[Spin (magazine)|Spin]]'' magazine's ranking of "The 30 Best '90s R&B Songs".

"Hold On" is a song by American girl group En Vogue, released in February 1990 by Atlantic Records as the first single from their debut album, Born to Sing (1990). It was produced by Denzil Foster and Thomas McElroy, and written by the former two and all members of the group. It peaked at number two on the US Billboard Hot 100 and topped the Billboard Dance Club Play, 12-inch Singles Sales, and Hot Black Singles charts. Internationally, "Hold On" entered the top 10 in the Netherlands, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. Its accompanying music video was directed by Tarsem Singh. En Vogue performed "Hold On" at the 2008 BET Awards with Alicia Keys. In 2017, it was ranked number four on Spin magazine's ranking of "The 30 Best '90s R&B Songs".

sections.heading: Production
sections.wikitext: The song opens with an [[a cappella]] rendition of the [[Motown]] standard "[[Who's Lovin' You]]", written by [[Smokey Robinson]] and originally recorded by his group, [[the Miracles]]. It features lead vocals by [[Cindy Herron]] and [[Terry Ellis]] vocals on the introduction.
sections.text: The song opens with an a cappella rendition of the Motown standard "Who's Lovin' You", written by Smokey Robinson and originally recorded by his group, the Miracles. It features lead vocals by Cindy Herron and Terry Ellis vocals on the introduction.

sections.heading: Critical reception
sections.wikitext:
David Taylor-Wilson from ''[[Bay Area Reporter]]'' complimented the song as "sexy and gentle, with a teasing, [[downtempo]] [[Electronic dance music|dance]] beat."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= David |last= Taylor-Wilson |title= Patti's Gonna Getcha |magazine= [[Bay Area Reporter]] |date= May 10, 1990 |page= 34 |access-date= April 23, 2020 |url= https://cdnc.ucr.edu/cgi-bin/cdnc?a=d&d=BAR19900510.1.34}}</ref> Bill Coleman from ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine wrote, "Step back and give 'em some room! Quartet of future divas fresh from the [[Denzil Foster|Foster]]/[[Thomas McElroy|McElroy]] stable deliver intricate, tight harmonies with a dash of sass on this groove-laden debut. Can't wait for the [[Born to Sing (En Vogue album)|album]]."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Bill|last=Coleman|url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/90s/1990/BB-1990-03-17.pdf|title=Single Reviews|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=March 17, 1990|page=93|access-date=January 25, 2018}}</ref> He also noted its "lazy and hypnotic [[Contemporary R&B|R&B]] pulse [that] serves as the perfect bed for the members' on-the-money styling; you would be doing your dancefloor a great disservice if you ignored it..."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Bill |last= Coleman |title= Dance Trax: R&B Tracks Provide A Slice Of 'Ghetto Heaven' |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date= April 21, 1990 |page= 25 |access-date= October 14, 2020 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Billboard/90s/1990/BB-1990-04-21.pdf}}</ref> Jan DeKnock from ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' felt En Vogue's "tasty harmonies are supported by an equally intoxicating groove."<ref>DeKnock, Jan (June 28, 1990). "Home Entertainment: Recordings". ''[[Chicago Tribune]]''. p. 7.</ref> A. Scott Galloway from ''The Network Forty'' wrote, "Gold single, golden girls! What more do you need to convince you to spin this hardcore dance floor jam."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=A. Scott|last=Galloway|url=https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Archive-Network-40/90/Network-40-1990-05-25.pdf|title=Crossover: Retail Sales|magazine=The Network Forty|date=May 25, 1990|page=38|access-date=March 21, 2020}}</ref> Gerald Martinez from ''[[New Sunday Times]]'' declared it as "[[Gospel (music)|gospel]]-[[funk]]" with "stunning vocal arrangements."<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Gerald|last=Martinez|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IJoWAAAAIBAJ|title=Top notch hits from Collins|magazine=[[New Sunday Times]]|date=November 15, 1998|page=13|access-date=March 12, 2020}}</ref>

In his album review, Edward Hill from ''[[The Plain Dealer]]'' remarked that "Hold On" "is already famous for its no-holds-barred a cappella opening and sluggishly powerful bassline. On [[12-inch]] it's pepped up with bonus beats and a slightly faster rhythm track."<ref>Hill, Edward (May 4, 1990). "En Vogue can wail with best girl groups". ''[[The Plain Dealer]]''.</ref> [[David Quantick]] from ''[[Smash Hits]]'' complimented it as "lithe and lovely".<ref>{{cite magazine|first=David|last=Quantick|url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/smashhits90s/25645009067/in/album-72157693156746214/|title=Review: LPs|magazine=[[Smash Hits]]|issue=300|page=60|date=May 30, 1990|access-date=March 9, 2020|author-link=David Quantick}}</ref> Steve Daly, writing for ''[[Spin (magazine)|Spin]]'' magazine, said the song is "perfect for those warm evening on the stoop", and felt that the "exotic melody takes its cue from [[Soul II Soul]], while the rhythm section does a slow grind in 95 percent humidity with no [[Air conditioning|AC]]."<ref name="SPIN">{{cite magazine|first=Steve|last=Daly|title=Singles|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=otG9qgDiY1cC&q=%22EN+VOGUE%22+%22HOLD+ON%22&pg=PA84|magazine=[[Spin (magazine)|Spin]]|date=August 1, 1990|access-date=February 25, 2018}}</ref> [[Cheo Hodari Coker|Cheo H. Coker]] from ''[[Stanford Daily]]'' wrote, "It was the first song in a long time that featured real singing, perfect four-part harmony (a capella no less), and a mother lode of hip-hop attitude and feeling."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Cheo H. |last= Coker |title= Hip-hop's four funky divas |magazine= [[Stanford Daily]] |date= April 16, 1992 |access-date= April 23, 2020 |url= https://archives.stanforddaily.com/1992/04/16 |author-link= Cheo Hodari Coker}}</ref> A reviewer from ''[[Wells Journal]]'' called it "a moody but repetitive song with mellow backing track".<ref>"Sounds of the studio". ''[[Wells Journal]]''. July 5, 1990. p. 72.</ref>
sections.text:
David Taylor-Wilson from Bay Area Reporter complimented the song as "sexy and gentle, with a teasing, downtempo dance beat." Bill Coleman from Billboard magazine wrote, "Step back and give 'em some room! Quartet of future divas fresh from the Foster/McElroy stable deliver intricate, tight harmonies with a dash of sass on this groove-laden debut. Can't wait for the album." He also noted its "lazy and hypnotic R&B pulse [that] serves as the perfect bed for the members' on-the-money styling; you would be doing your dancefloor a great disservice if you ignored it..." Jan DeKnock from Chicago Tribune felt En Vogue's "tasty harmonies are supported by an equally intoxicating groove." A. Scott Galloway from The Network Forty wrote, "Gold single, golden girls! What more do you need to convince you to spin this hardcore dance floor jam." Gerald Martinez from New Sunday Times declared it as "gospel-funk" with "stunning vocal arrangements."

In his album review, Edward Hill from The Plain Dealer remarked that "Hold On" "is already famous for its no-holds-barred a cappella opening and sluggishly powerful bassline. On 12-inch it's pepped up with bonus beats and a slightly faster rhythm track." David Quantick from Smash Hits complimented it as "lithe and lovely". Steve Daly, writing for Spin magazine, said the song is "perfect for those warm evening on the stoop", and felt that the "exotic melody takes its cue from Soul II Soul, while the rhythm section does a slow grind in 95 percent humidity with no AC." Cheo H. Coker from Stanford Daily wrote, "It was the first song in a long time that featured real singing, perfect four-part harmony (a capella no less), and a mother lode of hip-hop attitude and feeling." A reviewer from Wells Journal called it "a moody but repetitive song with mellow backing track".

sections.heading: Retrospective reviews
sections.wikitext: Retrospectively, [[AllMusic]] editor Jose F. Promis described the song as a "cool, shuffling, timeless [[Hip hop music|hip-hop]] [[Contemporary R&B|R&B]] track".<ref>{{cite web|first=Jose F.|last=Promis|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/born-to-sing-mw0000204202|title=En Vogue – Born to Sing|publisher=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=February 15, 2020}}</ref> Another editor, [[Stephen Thomas Erlewine]], described it as "yearning".<ref>{{cite web|first=Stephen Thomas|last=Erlewine|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/the-very-best-of-en-vogue-mw0000011510|title=En Vogue – The Very Best of En Vogue|publisher=[[AllMusic]]|access-date=March 23, 2020|author-link=Stephen Thomas Erlewine}}</ref> In 2007, Laura Checkoway from ''[[Vibe (magazine)|Vibe]]'' declared it as "an answer of sorts" to 1962's "[[Who's Lovin' You]]" from [[Smokey Robinson]] & [[The Miracles]].<ref>{{cite magazine|first=Laura|last=Checkoway|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qyYEAAAAMBAJ|title=ESSENTIAL EN VOGUE|magazine=[[Vibe (magazine)|Vibe]]|date=June 1, 2007|page=134|access-date=March 17, 2020}}{{Dead link|date=August 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
sections.text: Retrospectively, AllMusic editor Jose F. Promis described the song as a "cool, shuffling, timeless hip-hop R&B track". Another editor, Stephen Thomas Erlewine, described it as "yearning". In 2007, Laura Checkoway from Vibe declared it as "an answer of sorts" to 1962's "Who's Lovin' You" from Smokey Robinson & The Miracles.

sections.heading: Commercial performance
sections.wikitext: Following its release, "Hold On" peaked at number one on the US ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' [[Hot Black Singles]] chart, number two on ''Billboard''{{'}}s [[Hot 100]] on July 21, 1990, and number one on ''Billboard''{{'}}s [[Dance Club Songs|Dance Club Play]] and [[Dance Singles Sales|12-inch Singles Sales]] charts. "Hold On" was also a hit in several countries worldwide, reaching number five in the United Kingdom and New Zealand, number six in Germany, number 10 in the Netherlands, and number 12 in Austria. In West Asia, it became a top-20 hit in Israel, peaking at number 11 on June 10, 1990.<ref name="israel">{{cite web|url=https://israelcharts.com/|title=Israeli Charts|date=June 10, 1990|access-date=August 19, 2026|archive-date=June 26, 2026|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260626205604/https://israelcharts.com/|url-status=live}} Search "Hold On" for Israeli chart history.</ref> It was the top R&B hit on the [[Billboard Year-End|''Billboard'' Year-End]] chart for 1990 and was the eighth most-successful pop hit on the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 Year-End chart.<ref name="usr&bye"/><ref name="usye"/>
sections.text: Following its release, "Hold On" peaked at number one on the US Billboard Hot Black Singles chart, number two on Billboard{{'}}s Hot 100 on July 21, 1990, and number one on Billboard{{'}}s Dance Club Play and 12-inch Singles Sales charts. "Hold On" was also a hit in several countries worldwide, reaching number five in the United Kingdom and New Zealand, number six in Germany, number 10 in the Netherlands, and number 12 in Austria. In West Asia, it became a top-20 hit in Israel, peaking at number 11 on June 10, 1990. It was the top R&B hit on the Billboard Year-End chart for 1990 and was the eighth most-successful pop hit on the Billboard Hot 100 Year-End chart.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: A music video was produced to promote the single, directed by Indian director [[Tarsem Singh]].{{citation needed|date=December 2023}} It begins with a close-up of [[Terry Ellis]] singing the lead vocal of the intro, with the three other girls singing background vocals and standing either behind her or in front of her. They are all dressed in black. When the rhythm kicks in, several male dancers appear. [[Cindy Herron]] then takes over the lead vocal, standing in the front, with the three others backing her. The background dancers were filmed performing their dance moves slowly, and the footage was then sped up in the editing to match the song's rhythm. The effect gave the dancers a surreal sped-up quality. Actor/model [[Djimon Hounsou]] appears in the video as a trumpet player.

They are all dressed in black. When the rhythm kicks in, several male dancers appear. Cindy Herron then takes over the lead vocal, standing in the front, with the three others backing her. The effect gave the dancers a surreal sped-up quality. Actor/model Djimon Hounsou appears in the video as a trumpet player.

sections.heading: Impact and legacy
sections.wikitext: ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' ranked "Hold On" number 47 in their "Top 50 Dance Songs" list in 2015, adding, "[[R&B]] girl group En Vogue broke through with this club classic. A sharp acapella rendition of [[Motown]] standard '[[Who's Lovin' You|Who's Lovin You]]' leads into a [[Hip hop music|hip-hop]] beat with a funky bass line, horn and piano sounds. "''You've got to hold on, to your love''", the girls proclaim, and it is their powerful singing that carries this one."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/music/rockandpopmusic/11113077/Top-50-dance-songs.html|title=Top 50 dance songs|newspaper=The Daily Telegraph|access-date=March 7, 2017}}</ref> ''[[Spin (magazine)|Spin]]'' ranked the song number four in their list of "The 30 Best '90s R&B Songs" in 2017. They wrote, "Producers [[Denzil Foster|Foster]] & [[Thomas McElroy|McElroy]] deliver a slow-burning rhythm with a [[James Brown]] drum kick, but 'Hold On'{{'}}s greatest element is Herron, Terry Ellis, Dawn Robinson, and Maxine Jones blending their voices into a sound that shifts the culture."<ref>{{cite web|title=The 30 Best '90s R&B Songs|publisher=[[Spin (magazine)|Spin]]|url=https://www.spin.com/featured/30-best-90s-rnb-songs/|access-date=December 15, 2019}}</ref> In 2019, ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine ranked it number 130 in their list of "''Billboard''{{'}}s Top Songs of the '90s".<ref>{{cite magazine|first=|last=|title=Greatest of All Time: Billboard's Top Songs of the '90s|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|url=https://www.billboard.com/charts/greatest-billboards-top-songs-90s/|date=2019|accessdate=April 23, 2022}}</ref>
sections.text: The Daily Telegraph ranked "Hold On" number 47 in their "Top 50 Dance Songs" list in 2015, adding, "R&B girl group En Vogue broke through with this club classic. A sharp acapella rendition of Motown standard 'Who's Lovin You' leads into a hip-hop beat with a funky bass line, horn and piano sounds. "You've got to hold on, to your love", the girls proclaim, and it is their powerful singing that carries this one." Spin ranked the song number four in their list of "The 30 Best '90s R&B Songs" in 2017. They wrote, "Producers Foster & McElroy deliver a slow-burning rhythm with a James Brown drum kick, but 'Hold On'{{'}}s greatest element is Herron, Terry Ellis, Dawn Robinson, and Maxine Jones blending their voices into a sound that shifts the culture." In 2019, Billboard magazine ranked it number 130 in their list of "Billboard{{'}}s Top Songs of the '90s".
